Part Specs Have Changed - This is the part # for our 11 year old GE refrigerator but this auger's measurements are different than the part I was replacing. I had bought another, cheaper auger on Amazon that also had problems with measurements. Other users recommended grinding down the metal rod. I did not have a grinder so I returned that one. After installing this auger with all my original pieces it was binding some place. Couldn't see where. Auger would manually turn with extreme difficulty. I knew the motor could burn out if I reinstalled the housing it the way it was. I searched YouTube and checked the schematics for this part. My original auger had 2 metal washers plus a plastic spacer at the end closest to the plastic spirals. Different schematics showed either 2 plastic spacers or 1 plastic spacer; no metal washers I finally found a couple on YouTube that demonstrated the difference in measurements on their auger. They also had 2 metal washers. He was able to grind down the dent on the rod to allow all his original pieces to fit including the 2 metal washer. I was ready to return this auger as I did not have a grinder. I should not have to be a machinist to get a part to work. Taking a chance I put everything back on the rod in proper order except for the 2 metal washers. Everything works great. Ice cubes come out and cubes get crusher almost better than before. Have been using for about a week without any problems. Very happy except this took me much more time to figure out than required. Without this issue it would have taken less than 20 minutes for total install and a 5 star rating. Something in the specs for this auger has changed over the last 11 years.

Great quality, appearance and functionality. Installation was challenging. - Got this range hood to replace an over the range microwave/exhaust fan. It wasn’t something that would be visible after it was installed so I could live with it. It looks and works beautifully after I got it installed. I installed it myself which was mistake number one. Unless you are a serious do it your selfer, I recommend hiring someone to do the install and not just some handyman but an experienced appliance repairman. I added a photo of when the install was in process. I had to tap into the microwave electrical outlet box to run a wire out the wall for the hood as it is set up to be hard wired (no plug in cord included). I had to attach a couple of strips of wood under the cabinet to accept the screws to hang the hood on. I had to fight with the sheet metal ducting to get it to fit the hood properly. I screwed a couple of scrap boards into the unfinished side cabinets to support the hood while it was being jockeyed into place for the install and that made things a lot easier. There were trips to the hardware store for parts and even a special twelve inch extension for my drill in order to reach the support screws. There was also some sweating, a lot of cussing and some blood from minor lacerations. We are very happy with the end product. I loved the challenge and would do it again.

That seemed great, so I purchased it. I now see that these claims for this same filter are gone, and they recommend changing the filter at the regular time. (I'm just shaking my head...)

Finally, I don't know if it was a feature or using my filter for a year, but I had a horrible, terrible time getting their old filter out. The new filter went in fine; although the instructions didn't talk about running water through it, we ran about 10 quarts of water through it, and all has been well.

Kinda pricey understates it, no?
It's really a shortcut that, in the end, though stylish and handsome, is not necessary. Practice makes perfect. Items like this and steaming thermometers are aimed at new recruits in the coffee army who become frustrated during boot camp and finally want something that just works. Believe me, I understand, but immerse yourself in videos, online advice, and visit good coffee shops (no, not *$s!). Watch the baristas. Some shops offer classes. While it might seem silly to take a class in "milk chemistry" or such, it's not. You'll gain by watching, listening, and speaking with others trying to master the craft.

If you love the look of this pitcher, and I don't blame you if you do-- it's cool looking, for sure-- buy it. But if it's just that you're not having luck steaming milk with a new machine, keep working. Avoid gimmicks that promise you a no effort shortcut. In the end, you'll be a better barista if you just stick with it, get the advice and instruction you need, and finally (and you will) master producing creamy microfoam.

Cheers, mates.

Read everything - We are about a week into it and this machine works great so far. We have run about 3 gallons of water through it. However, there are a few things to note.

4) The "cleaning" mode doesn't seem to do a whole lot. The ad makes it look like it swirls, etc., but it just basically runs water through the system for a few minutes.

I can move a small amount of ice from the ramp into the bin and it will start again. Also, once the auto-shutoff is activated, it will allow about half of what is in it melt before it starts making ice automatically again unless you open and close the lid. This may be by design since they want you to remove all the ice to a freezer.
6) I thought there was a light in it but there is not. That's an aesthetic thing to me and probably wouldn't bother most people.

Also, when I originally purchased it, it said it wouldn't ship until November but it shipped in less than a week.

Try a bucket and a plunger, first - Was excited to get this product. After doing my first two loads, I'm honestly underwhelmed. Got it together, no problem. Put it on a table outside, so I could grab the gray water in a bucket and water the plants. I put in water, soap (which I measured according to their instructions), a little baking soda because of our hard water, and a 2 lb load of light pajamas and undies. Spun it at the right speed -- and heard flop, flop, flop, instead of splash, splash, splash. The lump of wet clothes doesn't mix at all, it just flops from one side to the other in a clump.

Ok. Maybe that's ok. Released the lid, swished with my hand for a minute, then put in the drain pipe. Water spilled onto the table. Glad it had a plastic cloth on it. Drained into the bucket. Refilled, added some vinegar, did the whole thing again to rinse. Rinsed a second time. Still bubbly water. Stood there with the hose running into the pot while it drained at the same time, swishing with my hand. Finally ran clear. Took the pieces one at a time and ran them through my salad spinner to get rid of a lot of the water, then hung to dry.

The clothes look clean, except for one major problem. We have lots of animals, which means lots of fur. Fur gets removed in the regular washer and dryer. It does not get removed with this.

I may try making "washer rings" out of some of plastic needlepoint canvas, and see if tossing some of those in to break up the lump of laundry will help. Or try using dryer balls. Otherwise, I think this will go back and I'll get one of the plunger types and a 5 gallon bucket. Or forget the whole thing and go back to the regular washer.
